doc.title: Bruce Johnstone interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2013

title: Lessons from Maynard, Woody and Buddy Rich
summary: Maynard paced his playing and built followings for soloists; Woody was fiscally irresponsible; Buddy Rich withheld pay yet produced great players.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: What did you learn from those guys? Maynard or Woody. I mean, beyond the music.

I learned about working a crowd. Maynard didn’t play on everything. He said you can only amaze people once. So that’s why he surrounded himself with young players who could play. And he would build a following for each of his prime soloists. So people © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

would come to see you, as well as Maynard. Because Maynard didn’t really play hard on everything, it was just a few things. And he would space it just beautifully. And he just was a very personable guy. And the audiences really loved him. And it was great. He could whip up a crowd to a frenzy in a flash. It was wonderful. Woody was fiscally irresponsible unfortunately. He was taken advantage of by a lot of people, and in fact I think Artie Shaw bought his house so that Woody wouldn’t have to lose it.
Yeah, he was like deeply in debt to the government.

Horrible, horrible. But he would do things, he would drop us in a bus at some ratty hotel and then he’d go on to live at a much higher up the food chain type hotel. Either that or Buddy Rich. Buddy would not pay his guys for three or four weeks. So they were all indebted to him because they wanted the money that they’d already earned. And yet some of the greatest players in the world have come out of the “Buddy Rich School of Boot Camp.” And they all loved him. They all loved him. And they all admired and respected him, even though he did stomp on them a little bit.
